intro.html: There are many ways to stop something. You can scare it off before it starts, talk someone out of it, hold it in check, cut it short, press it down or crush it flat. Each word in this topic names one of those ways.

Before it starts: deter (discourage, often by fear), dissuade (talk out of). Keeping it in check: curb (restrain), curtail (cut short). Pressing it down: repress, suppress, stifle. Crushing it: quash, squelch. Stopping a flow: stanch.
Three of these words share a Latin verb, premere, to press: re-press (press back), sup-press (press under) and, in a roundabout way, the everyday press itself.

words.def: to discourage someone from acting, often through fear of what might happen
words.ex: The barking dog {deters} anyone from climbing over the fence.
words.ctx: The town hoped bright new streetlights would {deter} vandals, since people are less likely to cause trouble where they can easily be seen.
words.etym: From Latin deterrere, “to frighten away”: de- (away) + terrere (to frighten).

mn.text: Felix dresses up as a scarecrow, and the crows flap off in terror; the scary sight {deters} them from the corn.

scene.alt: A man dressed as a scarecrow shouts “Boo!” and two crows fly away in fright.

words.def: to talk someone out of doing something
words.ex: Nothing could {dissuade} Maya from trying out for the team.
words.ctx: Jonah planned to hike the trail alone after dark, but his sister {dissuaded} him by pointing out the steep cliffs and the lack of cell service.
words.etym: From Latin dissuadere: dis- (away) + suadere (to urge).

mn.text: Dev wants to paint his room neon orange, but Dad talks him out of it: Dad {dissuades} him.

labels.text: DIS-SUADE: talk him OUT of it

scene.alt: A teen holds up a paintbrush over a bucket of orange paint while his father waves his hands, talking him out of it.

words.def: to hold back or keep under control
words.ex: The library posted a new rule to {curb} noise after six o’clock.
words.ctx: To {curb} her spending, Lin left her credit card at home and carried only enough cash for the groceries on her list.
words.etym: From French courbe, “curved,” first the curved strap or chain on a horse’s bit that holds the horse in check.

mn.text: Pip wants to dash after his ball, but Mom holds him back at the curb until the cars pass: she {curbs} his rush.

scene.alt: A mother holds her son back at the curb while a car passes and his ball sits in the street.

words.def: to cut short or cut back
words.ex: Rain {curtailed} the game after only three innings.
words.ctx: Because the bridge was closed for repairs, the bus company had to {curtail} its route, ending at the river instead of crossing into town.
words.etym: From an old word, curtal, “with a docked tail,” from French court (short); the spelling was later shaped by tail.

mn.text: Ten minutes into the picnic, a storm rolls in and snips the afternoon short like a tail: the rain {curtails} the picnic.

scene.alt: A storm cloud cuts a riverside picnic short as a man and a girl hurry to pack up.

words.def: to hold back or keep down, especially a feeling
words.ex: Dev had to {repress} a laugh when the principal’s microphone squeaked.
words.ctx: For years she {repressed} her wish to become an artist, hiding her sketchbooks in a drawer, until a teacher saw them and urged her to apply to art school.
words.etym: From Latin reprimere, “to press back”: re- (back) + premere (to press).

mn.text: Kai’s block tower crashes, and he feels the anger rising, but he presses it back down and takes a slow breath: he {represses} it.

scene.alt: A boy whose block tower has fallen holds his anger in, steaming but saying he is fine.

words.def: to put down by force; to keep from being seen or known
words.ex: The firefighters worked all night to {suppress} the brush fire.
words.ctx: The company tried to {suppress} the report about its faulty toasters, but a worker shared it, and soon every customer knew.
words.etym: From Latin supprimere, “to press under”: sub- (under) + premere (to press).

mn.text: Omar pours bucket after bucket until the campfire is pressed down to nothing: he {suppresses} the flames.

scene.alt: A man in a helmet pours a bucket of water on a campfire, putting it out.

words.def: to hold back, as a yawn or a laugh; also, to smother
words.ex: Grandpa {stifled} a yawn during the long speech.
words.ctx: Too many strict rules can {stifle} creativity; when every drawing has to look the same, students stop trying new ideas.

mn.cue: a STIFF hand: STIF-le the yawn
mn.text: In the middle of the long concert, Professor Edwin clamps a stiff hand over his mouth to hold in a giant yawn: he {stifles} it.

scene.alt: An old professor presses a hand over his mouth to hold in a yawn while a violinist plays.

words.def: to put a complete stop to; to cancel officially
words.ex: The coach {quashed} the rumor that the team was moving to another city.
words.ctx: The higher court {quashed} the earlier ruling, declaring it invalid, so the case had to be heard again from the very beginning.

mn.text: The judge brings her gavel down on the unfair rule and squashes it flat: she {quashes} it.

scene.alt: A judge raises her gavel to squash an unfair rule.

words.ex: Mom {squelched} our plan to build a ramp off the garage roof.
words.ctx: The manager’s harsh reply {squelched} any further questions; after that, no one at the meeting dared to raise a hand.

mn.cue: SQUELCH! like a boot in the mud
mn.text: Rex starts a silly rumor, and Lin stomps on it at once, squelch, like a boot in deep mud: she {squelches} it.

scene.alt: A woman stomps a rumor into the mud while the man who started it looks shocked.

words.def: to stop the flow of a liquid
words.ex: The plumber hurried to {stanch} the flood from the broken pipe.
words.ctx: Volunteers piled sandbags along the riverbank to {stanch} the water pouring over the low wall, and by morning the flow had stopped.
words.etym: From Old French estanchier, “to stop the flow of.”
words.note: Also spelled staunch. As an adjective, staunch means loyal and firm: a staunch friend.

mn.text: Water gushes from a hole in the rain barrel, and Sven slaps his hand over it to stop the flow: he {stanches} the leak.

scene.alt: A big man presses his hand over a hole in a leaking barrel to stop the water.

after.html: dissuade is the opposite of persuade: to persuade is to talk someone into something, and to dissuade is to talk someone out of it. stanch (stop a flow) is also spelled staunch, which as an adjective means loyal.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: Her friends tried to {dissuade} her from quitting the band, reminding her how much she loved the drums.

after.cap: Talking someone out of something is dissuading.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of persuade?
items.why: To persuade is to talk someone into something; to dissuade is to talk someone out of it. Deter is close, but it often works through fear rather than talk.

items.q: True or false: stanch and staunch can both mean to stop the flow of a liquid.
items.why: True. Staunch is another spelling of the verb. As an adjective, staunch also means loyal.

items.q: The storm forced the school to cut the field trip from five days to two. The storm ______ the trip.
items.why: To cut something short is to curtail it.

choices: The tall fence deters deer from eating the lettuce.
The tall fence deters the lettuce to grow.
She deterred her friend into joining the team.
items.why: To deter is to discourage someone from doing something. You deter someone from an action.
